description: The bar chart illustrates the negative log probability of per-specialty terms when a model is fine-tuned on different clinical specialties, as explored in the paper “What Does Neuro Mean to Cardio? Investigating the Role of Clinical Specialty Data in Medical LLMs.” The vertical axis represents “Negative log probability,” ranging from approximately -22 to -27, with lower values indicating higher model confidence (i.e., lower uncertainty) in predicting the term. The horizontal axis lists six medical specialties — Cardio, Gastro, Infect, Neuro, Obstetrics, and Pediatrics — each corresponding to a group of six vertical bars. Each bar within a group represents the model’s performance when fine-tuned on one of the six specialties (indicated by the legend: Cardio = light orange, Gastro = medium orange, Infect = dark orange, Neuro = brown, Obstetrics = dark brown, Pediatrics = darkest brown). A light blue bar, labeled in the legend as “Fine-tuned on:” (with the actual label obscured), appears consistently as the first bar in each group, likely representing a baseline or control condition (e.g., fine-tuned on a general or mixed dataset). Across all specialty groups, the bars vary in height, reflecting differences in model uncertainty depending on the fine-tuning specialty. For example, in the “Cardio” group, the “Cardio”-fine-tuned model (light orange) shows the lowest negative log probability (highest confidence), while the “Pediatrics”-fine-tuned model (darkest brown) shows the highest negative log probability (lowest confidence). A similar pattern is generally observed across other groups: models fine-tuned on the same specialty as the test terms tend to perform best (lowest negative log probability), while those fine-tuned on unrelated specialties perform worse. The chart visually supports the paper’s investigation into how specialty-specific training affects a model’s understanding of domain-specific terminology, revealing that fine-tuning on a given specialty improves performance on its own terms, suggesting some degree of specialization and potential lack of generalization across domains.
